newsitem.title: USA: Mitsubishi sets workplace plan for Illinois plant.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi sets workplace plan for Illinois plant.

text.p: Mitsubishi Motor Manufacturing of America Inc., whose Illinois car plant is the object of a federal sexual harassment lawsuit, unveiled its plan Wednesday to educate the factory's nearly 4,300 workers.

Special consultant Lynn Martin, a former U.S. Secretary of Labour hired by Mitsubishi nine months ago, presented a 48-page report outlining dozens of recommendations and goals that she said pointed toward "zero tolerance" of sexual harassment or discrimination at the Normal, Ill., plant.
Martin said workers and managers at the central Illinois plant were briefed on the plan Tuesday, and she described their reaction to it as "guarded."

Tsuneo Ohinouye, chairman and CEO of the U.S. arm of Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp., commented sparingly to reporters on the lawsuit brought nearly a year ago by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission on behalf of potentially hundreds of female workers who were allegedly sexually harassed.
"To make a resolution (of the lawsuit), we need to know the facts. That's why we're trying to expedite the discovery process," Ohinouye said at a news conference.

Officials from the company's Japanese parent have said they want a quick settlement of the federal lawsuit, which the U.S. agency has said is potentially the largest case of its kind ever brought and could result in hundreds of millions of dollars in damage awards.

Ohinouye said the company had also spoken to lawyers for 11 of the more than two dozen women who together filed a seperate civil suit charging sexual harassment, prior to the federal lawsuit. He said discussions centred on whether the women who resigned might return to work at the plant.

Both Ohinouye and Martin sought to portray the problems at the plant more as a breakdown in communication between management, workers and the United Auto Workers union, which they planned to remedy whatever the cost.
"There was a seperation of management from the people who work there," Martin said. "What we heard most often (from workers) was, 'It's not consistent, it's not fair.'"

Already, all of the plant's 4,256 workers had undergone training in avoiding sexual harassment and the company was hiring additional human relations experts to patrol the factory floor, Martin said. Cross-cultural training to educate American and Japanese workers about each other's cultures was also planned.
